note: Generalised deploy manual: one card per selectable flow. No benchmark_history side -- guidance is design-agnostic and must not encode per-benchmark results.

auto_pblock.description: Measures per-path max Manhattan distance between consecutive placed cells over the 50 worst paths, sizes a region for 1.5x the design's used LUT/FF/DSP/BRAM counts, picks the best contiguous fabric region avoiding delay-heavy columns, then unplaces the ENTIRE design, applies the region as a HARD pblock over the whole design, and re-places and re-routes from scratch.
use_when: critical-path spread is measurably large: the flow's own analysis labels average max consecutive-cell distance above 30 tiles as pblock-recommended, so states well above that line are the mechanism's actual target

the incumbent placement is disposable: because the flow starts from a full unplace, it is the right move when the current placement is believed bad and the wrong move when it embodies previously banked gains
utilization is low relative to the device: region targets are 1.5x used resources, so ample headroom lets the fabric search find a compact feasible region with margin
avoid_when: reapplying to a state this flow already produced: the mechanism unconditionally discards all placement (including its own previous result) and re-runs the placer -- there is no incremental mode, so a second application is a fresh placer run minus the already-banked win

high utilization or a resource mix dominated by column-bound hard blocks: a hard (non-soft) pblock sized at 1.5x must still contain enough BRAM/DSP columns, and tight fits recreate congestion inside the region

assuming the flow self-gates: the greater-than-30-tiles recommendation does NOT gate execution -- the flow proceeds to unplace even when its own analysis prints 'may not help', and if region analysis fails it still unplaces and re-places with no pblock at all (a plain full re-place); the caller must apply the spread check itself
auto_pblock.ceiling_note: The only live flow that re-runs global placement, so it has the largest reachable state change of any flow in either direction; every other live flow is a bounded set of physical-optimization moves on failing paths.

congestion_spread.description: Captures report_design_analysis -congestion before and after, but the report is informational only: the actual optimization is a single phys_opt_design pass with placement_opt + critical_cell_opt + clock_opt + slr_crossing_opt, followed by a re-route.
use_when: failing paths that local cell moves and critical-cell replication can improve: every transform in the bundle is a Vivado physical-optimization option that acts on failing paths and commits only timing-improving changes, so the blast radius is small
broad shallow violations where clock skew or replication tweaks can recover margin across many endpoints at once
avoid_when: expecting congestion-driven re-placement: no spreading, cell inflation, or region move is derived from the congestion report -- it is captured but never read by the optimization itself, so the flow name oversells the mechanism
on a single-die (single-SLR) target device: slr_crossing_opt has nothing to act on there, shrinking the bundle to a generic placement/cell-opt subset
congestion_spread.ceiling_note: Mechanically a subset-strength variant of generic physical optimization -- expect the same bounded incremental profile, not congestion-scale relief.

fanout.description: Reports timing in Vivado, asks for critical high-fanout nets over the 50 worst paths with a minimum fanout of 100, then loads the checkpoint into RapidWright and applies a fanout optimisation to each of the top nets (default 5, set by max_nets). RapidWright writes a new checkpoint, Vivado reads it back and re-routes the design, and WNS is compared against the starting point.
use_when: the diagnostic's fanout block shows real high-fanout structure: the flow only acts on nets above fanout 100 that appear on the 50 worst paths, so num_high_fanout_nets and max_fanout are the signals that it has anything to work on at all
critical paths are routing-dominated and the driver of a widely-shared net is a plausible cause, rather than logic depth on a narrow path
phys_opt has not already been applied to this state: its own fanout replication pass covers overlapping ground, so this flow has most to add on a state phys_opt has not seen
avoid_when: no net clears the fanout-100 threshold on the 50 worst paths: the flow will complete having changed effectively nothing, and still pay the full re-route cost
the state already came from phys_opt: the two mechanisms overlap on fanout replication, and this flow was long excluded from the live catalogue on exactly that assumption

an intact placement is worth protecting: this is the only live flow that round-trips the design out to RapidWright and back before a full re-route, so it carries structural risk the pure-Vivado flows do not
fanout.ceiling_note: Carries the joint-lowest base prior in the deterministic scorer (0.5, level with pblock, against 3.0 for phys_opt), and is the only live flow whose mechanism depends on a working RapidWright installation plus a full re-route. Expect a narrow, structure-dependent gain rather than a broad one.

hardblock_relocate.description: Counts RAMB/DSP/URAM cells on the 50 worst paths (a diagnostic print only -- the count does not branch), then runs phys_opt placement_opt + critical_cell_opt + dsp/bram/uram register opts, re-routes, and finishes with a placement/routing cleanup pass. Despite the name, it never moves a hard block: BRAM/DSP columns are fixed, and only surrounding registers and cells move.
use_when: hard blocks actually sit on failing paths: the register-opt options act on registers at BRAM/DSP/URAM boundaries, so nonzero DSP/BRAM utilization AND hard blocks on the worst paths is the precondition for this flow doing anything its generic siblings would not
avoid_when: hard-block-free failing paths: with nothing at hard-block boundaries the flow degenerates to placement_opt + critical_cell_opt, a strictly weaker generic physical-optimization pass

selecting it for macro relocation: the mechanism cannot relocate a hard block, only improve locality of the soft logic around it -- if the problem is a hard block placed far from its logic, the placement-scale flow is the one that can actually change that
hardblock_relocate.ceiling_note: Bounded by how much of the worst-path delay is registers/logic at hard-block boundaries; it inherits phys_opt's commit-only-if-improving safety.

lut_cone.description: Extracts pin-level data for the 20 worst paths, selects up to 30 LUT input pins, and has RapidWright's LUTInputConeOpt merge chained small LUTs into single wider (up to 6-input) LUTs. The modified checkpoint is then written by RAPIDWRIGHT's native writer (not Vivado), reopened in Vivado, and re-routed -- with no re-placement step.
use_when: worst paths are chains of small LUTs whose combined fan-in fits within 6 inputs (the merge precondition), and logic depth rather than route distance is the dominant delay component
verification budget exists downstream: this is the only live flow that edits the logical netlist, so functional-equivalence risk is intrinsic to the mechanism rather than incidental
avoid_when: route-dominated failing paths: merging shortens the logical chain, but merged LUTs are not re-placed -- only re-routed -- so wire-length problems survive the transform

anywhere checkpoint integrity matters more than upside: the output DCP comes from RapidWright's own serializer, the exact non-Vivado writer path behind the project's documented checkpoint-corruption bug (Vivado integrity-check warning on reopen; in sibling flows this sometimes silently dropped every LUT in the design)
expecting large-scale restructuring: the candidate list is capped at 30 pins per application, bounding how much depth can be removed in one run
lut_cone.ceiling_note: Each successful merge removes roughly one LUT-plus-net delay level on one path; the 30-pin cap and the merge fan-in limit keep the per-application ceiling small even in the best case.

memory_path_opt.description: A phys_opt pass with bram_register_opt + dsp_register_opt + uram_register_opt + bram_enable_opt + critical_pin_opt + equ_drivers_opt + placement_opt, a re-route, then a pin/driver/routing cleanup pass.
use_when: failing paths cross BRAM/DSP/URAM boundaries where hard-block registers can be moved or enables optimized: the four memory-specific options only fire there, and nonzero DSP-plus-BRAM utilization is the cheap observable proxy for that precondition
avoid_when: DSP and BRAM utilization are both zero: all four memory-specific options are no-ops by construction and the flow degenerates to its pin/driver/placement subset -- effectively a slightly heavier net_swap at higher runtime

hard-block registers are already optimally placed/enabled from a previous application: the options move existing registers rather than creating pipeline stages, so there is a one-time budget of movable registers
memory_path_opt.ceiling_note: Gains concentrate where a hard-block interface is the actual worst path; elsewhere the mechanism reduces to small pin/driver cleanup.

net_swap.display_name: LUT pin mapping and equivalent-driver rewiring
net_swap.description: Two targeted phys_opt passes -- critical_pin_opt + equ_drivers_opt with placement_opt on the first pass and routing_opt on the second -- with a re-route in between. No netlist restructure, no unplace, Vivado-native end to end.
use_when: small residual gaps on almost any state: LUT input-pin permutation and equivalent-driver rewiring are the lowest-blast-radius transforms in the live set, acting only on failing paths and committing only improving changes
avoid_when: gaps that need placement- or netlist-scale change: a pin permutation cannot move a cell, and per-swap delay differences are tiny, so this cannot close a large WNS deficit
states with no failing paths: every transform is gated on negative slack, so expect a no-op
net_swap.ceiling_note: Smallest per-move effect of the live flows by construction; the compensating property is that the mechanism has essentially no way to make the design worse.

phys_opt.description: phys_opt_design -directive Explore, a full route_design, then a second Explore pass. All transforms target failing paths, and Vivado commits a change only if timing improves.
use_when: as the default probe on any state with failing paths: the Explore directive covers fanout replication, critical-cell replication, register moves, and routing-aware placement moves -- the broadest transform coverage among the non-structural flows
when a safe, bounded improvement is worth more than a risky large one: the commit-only-if-improving loop makes meaningful degradation mechanically unlikely
avoid_when: the state already meets timing: transforms are gated on failing paths, so expect a no-op
immediately repeating it on its own output: the first pass already committed every improving move its search found, so a re-run explores an already-harvested space
phys_opt.ceiling_note: Incremental by construction -- local moves on failing paths with a route refresh -- so it cannot deliver placement-scale change; its distinctive property is breadth plus safety, not magnitude.

retime.description: A place_design call (incremental on an already-placed state), then a single phys_opt_design -directive AlternateFlowWithRetiming (more aggressive replication, DSP/BRAM register optimization, and register retiming), then a re-route.
use_when: register-imbalance states: worst paths fail while adjacent pipeline stages have slack to donate, which is the one situation the retiming transform can exploit and the other directives cannot
avoid_when: expecting information independent of generic physical optimization: this flow is the same phys_opt_design engine one directive apart, so on states where the retimer finds nothing to move the two flows can produce identical results -- treat them as correlated probes, not independent ones
paths bounded by fixed elements (I/O, hard-block boundaries without movable registers): the retimer needs registers that are free to cross combinational logic
retime.ceiling_note: Bounded by the slack imbalance between adjacent stages -- retiming redistributes slack rather than creating it, and the rest of the directive's moves overlap generic physical optimization.
